label: PYQ-style
stem: Describe the life cycle of Plasmodium, naming its two hosts and where sexual and asexual stages occur.
hint: Human: liver, RBC; mosquito: gut, salivary glands.
model_answer: *How much to write: 6–8 lines or a labelled cycle · 6 minutes* 1. A female *Anopheles* mosquito bites and injects sporozoites (the infectious form) into the human. 2. The parasites multiply asexually in liver cells, then attack red blood cells and multiply there, causing them to rupture. 3. Ruptured RBCs release haemozoin, which causes chill and high fever recurring every 3–4 days. 4. Some parasites form gametocytes (sexual stages) in the blood. 5. When a female *Anopheles* bites the patient, the gametocytes enter the mosquito; fertilisation and development take place in the mosquito's stomach (gut). 6. Sporozoites formed move to the mosquito's salivary glands, ready for the next bite. **Hosts:** human (asexual stages) and female *Anopheles* mosquito (sexual stage). :::tip Your answer must contain - sporozoites → liver → RBCs; haemozoin → fever - gametocytes; fertilisation in the mosquito gut; salivary glands - asexual in human, sexual in mosquito ::: **Marks are lost for:** reversing the hosts' roles; saying the male mosquito transmits malaria.

label: PYQ-style
stem: *Every spring, a student starts sneezing, gets watery eyes and a running nose whenever she walks past flowering trees. Her doctor says her immune system is over-reacting to something harmless and prescribes a tablet. Her brother had chickenpox as a child and never got it again.*

parts.stem: Name the condition and the class of antibody involved.
parts.model_answer: Allergy (to pollen, an allergen); IgE antibodies.

parts.stem: Which cells release the chemicals that cause her symptoms, and what are the chemicals?
parts.model_answer: Mast cells release histamine and serotonin.

parts.stem: Explain why the brother did not get chickenpox again, naming the type of immunity.
parts.model_answer: Acquired (active) immunity has memory: the first infection produced a primary response and memory cells; on re-exposure a rapid, intense secondary (anamnestic) response destroys the virus before disease develops.

scheme.step: Secondary (anamnestic) response is faster and stronger

hint: An exaggerated response to pollen involves one antibody class and one kind of cell. Then: what does the immune system remember?
model_answer:
*How much to write: one line each for (i) and (ii), 3 lines for (iii) · 6 minutes*

**(i)** <mark>Allergy</mark>: an exaggerated response of the immune system to an allergen (here pollen). The antibodies produced are of the <mark>IgE</mark> type.

**(ii)** <u>Mast cells</u> release chemicals such as <mark>histamine and serotonin</mark>, which cause sneezing, watery eyes and a running nose. (Anti-histamines, adrenalin and steroids reduce the symptoms.)

**(iii)** <mark>Acquired (active) immunity</mark> has <u>memory</u>. The first chickenpox infection produced a low-intensity <u>primary response</u> and memory cells. On re-exposure, a highly intensified <mark>secondary (anamnestic) response</mark> destroys the virus quickly, before disease can develop.

:::tip Your answer must contain
- (i) <mark>allergy</mark>, <mark>IgE</mark>
- (ii) <u>mast cells</u>, histamine and serotonin
- (iii) acquired immunity, <u>memory</u>, secondary response
:::

**Marks are lost for:** naming IgG in (i); calling the brother's protection innate immunity.

label: PYQ-style
stem:
(a) Distinguish between innate and acquired immunity. Describe the four types of barriers of innate immunity with an example each. [3]
(b) Distinguish between humoral and cell-mediated immunity. [2]
hint: Physical, physiological, cellular, cytokine.
model_answer:
*How much to write: about two-thirds of a page · 9 minutes*

**(a)**

| Innate immunity | Acquired immunity |
|---|---|
| <mark>non-specific</mark>; present at birth | <mark>pathogen-specific</mark>; develops after contact |
| no memory | has <u>memory</u> (primary and secondary responses) |

**Barriers of innate immunity:**
1. **Physical:** <u>skin</u>; <u>mucus coating</u> of the respiratory, gastrointestinal and urogenital tracts traps microbes.
2. **Physiological:** <u>acid in the stomach</u>, saliva in the mouth, tears from the eyes.
3. **Cellular:** leucocytes such as <u>neutrophils (PMNL), monocytes, natural killer cells</u> and macrophages phagocytose and destroy microbes.
4. **Cytokine:** virus-infected cells secrete <mark>interferons</mark>, which protect non-infected cells from further viral infection.

**(b)**

| Humoral immunity | Cell-mediated immunity (CMI) |
|---|---|
| mediated by <mark>antibodies made by B-lymphocytes</mark>, found in the blood | mediated by <mark>T-lymphocytes</mark>, without antibodies |
| fights pathogens in body fluids | responsible for <u>graft rejection</u> |

:::tip Your answer must contain
- innate vs acquired (specificity, memory)
- <u>four barriers</u>, each with an example
- humoral = <mark>B cells, antibodies</mark>; CMI = <mark>T cells</mark>, graft rejection
:::

**Marks are lost for:** listing only three barriers; giving antibodies as a cellular barrier; reversing B and T cells.

label: PYQ-style
stem: What does AIDS stand for? Describe how HIV multiplies in the human body and explain why an infected person becomes immunodeficient.
hint: Macrophage first, then reverse transcription, then helper T cells.
model_answer:
*How much to write: 7–9 lines · 6 minutes*

**AIDS:** <u>Acquired Immuno Deficiency Syndrome</u>, caused by <u>HIV</u>, a <u>retrovirus</u> with an RNA genome.

**Multiplication:**
1. HIV enters a <mark>macrophage</mark>.
2. Its RNA is copied into viral DNA by the enzyme <mark>reverse transcriptase</mark>.
3. The viral DNA <u>joins the host cell's DNA</u> and directs the cell to make virus particles: the macrophage becomes an "<u>HIV factory</u>".
4. New viruses enter <u>helper T-lymphocytes (T<sub>H</sub>)</u>, multiply and are released, attacking more T<sub>H</sub> cells.

**Immunodeficiency:** the <mark>number of helper T cells falls progressively</mark>. As T<sub>H</sub> cells are needed for both antibody and cell-mediated responses, the person cannot fight even ordinary infections and gets <u>opportunistic infections</u> (bacteria such as *Mycobacterium*, viruses, fungi, parasites such as *Toxoplasma*). Diagnosis is by <u>ELISA</u>.

:::tip Your answer must contain
- the full form and <u>retrovirus</u>
- <mark>macrophage → reverse transcriptase → viral DNA in host DNA</mark>
- <mark>fall in helper T cells</mark> → opportunistic infections
:::

**Marks are lost for:** saying HIV attacks B cells or red blood cells; leaving out reverse transcriptase.

scheme.step: Full form; HIV a retrovirus enters macrophage
Helper T cells decrease → immunodeficiency, opportunistic infections

label: PYQ-style
stem: Name the causative organism and give two symptoms each of (a) typhoid, (b) pneumonia and (c) filariasis.
hint: One bacterium that lives in the intestine, one that infects the alveoli, and a worm that lives in lymphatic vessels.
model_answer:
*How much to write: three short paragraphs · 5 minutes*

**(a) Typhoid** — <mark>*Salmonella typhi*</mark> (bacterium). Sustained high fever (39–40 °C), weakness, stomach pain, constipation, headache, loss of appetite; intestinal perforation in severe cases.

**(b) Pneumonia** — <mark>*Streptococcus pneumoniae*</mark> and *Haemophilus influenzae* (bacteria). Alveoli fill with fluid, so breathing is difficult; fever, chills, cough, headache; lips and finger nails may turn grey to bluish.

**(c) Filariasis (elephantiasis)** — <mark>*Wuchereria bancrofti* / *W. malayi*</mark> (filarial worms). Chronic inflammation of the <u>lymphatic vessels of the lower limbs</u>; gross deformities of the limbs and genital organs.

Typhoid is confirmed by the <u>Widal test</u>; filariasis is spread by the bite of <u>female mosquito vectors</u>.

:::tip Your answer must contain
- the correct <mark>genus and species</mark> for each
- two symptoms per disease
:::

**Marks are lost for:** writing "virus" for typhoid or pneumonia; naming *Ascaris* for filariasis.

label: PYQ-style
stem:
(a) How does a normal cell become a cancer cell? Distinguish between benign and malignant tumours, and name two kinds of carcinogens. [2]
(b) Describe the methods used to detect and treat cancer. [3]
hint: (a) Contact inhibition is lost. (b) Detection: biopsy, imaging, antibodies, molecular tests. Treatment: surgery, radiation, chemotherapy, immunotherapy.
model_answer:
*How much to write: about one page · 10 minutes*

**(a)** Normal cells show <u>contact inhibition</u>: contact with other cells stops their growth. <mark>Cancer cells lose this property</mark>, divide uncontrollably and form masses called <u>tumours</u>.
- **Benign tumours** stay confined to their original location and cause little damage.
- **Malignant tumours** grow rapidly, invade surrounding tissue and spread through the blood to distant sites (<mark>metastasis</mark>).
- **Carcinogens:** physical (<u>ionising radiation</u> such as X-rays and γ-rays; <u>non-ionising UV</u>), chemical (<u>tobacco smoke</u>), biological (<u>oncogenic viruses</u>). Cellular oncogenes (c-onc), when activated, also cause transformation.

**(b) Detection:**
- <u>Biopsy and histopathology</u>: a piece of suspected tissue is cut into thin sections, stained and examined; blood and bone-marrow tests show increased cell counts in leukaemia.
- <u>Radiography (X-rays), CT and MRI</u> detect cancers of internal organs.
- <u>Antibodies against cancer-specific antigens</u>; <u>molecular biology techniques</u> detect genes that make a person prone to certain cancers.

**Treatment:**
- <u>Surgery</u>, <u>radiation therapy</u> (tumour cells irradiated lethally, normal tissue protected) and <u>chemotherapy</u> (drugs that kill cancer cells; side effects such as hair loss and anaemia). Most cancers are treated with a combination.
- <mark>Immunotherapy</mark>: biological response modifiers such as <u>α-interferon</u> activate the immune system to destroy the tumour.

:::tip Your answer must contain
- loss of <mark>contact inhibition</mark>
- benign vs malignant with <u>metastasis</u>
- two carcinogen types
- detection: <u>biopsy</u>, imaging, antibodies
- treatment: surgery, radiation, chemotherapy, <mark>α-interferon</mark>
:::

**Marks are lost for:** not mentioning contact inhibition; calling a benign tumour cancerous; leaving out immunotherapy.

scheme.step: Loss of contact inhibition; benign vs malignant (metastasis)

label: PYQ-style
stem: Explain how a vaccine produces active immunity. Why does a second dose of the same vaccine give a faster and stronger response?
hint: The body makes its own antibodies and keeps memory cells.
model_answer:
*How much to write: 6–7 lines · 5 minutes*

A vaccine contains a <u>weakened or killed pathogen</u>, or only its <u>antigen</u>. The body treats it as foreign: <u>B-lymphocytes</u> are activated and make <mark>specific antibodies</mark> (the <u>primary response</u>). Some activated cells remain as <u>memory B and T cells</u>.

On a second dose the <u>memory cells</u> recognise the antigen at once, so the <mark>secondary response is faster and stronger</mark>: more antibodies are made in less time. This is why <u>booster doses</u> are given.

:::tip Your answer must contain
- the vaccine's <u>antigen</u> and the body's own <u>antibodies</u> (active immunity)
- <mark>memory cells</mark> that persist after the first dose
- the second dose: <mark>faster and stronger</mark> response
:::

**Marks are lost for:** saying the vaccine gives ready-made antibodies (that is passive immunity); not linking the faster response to memory cells.

scheme.step: Vaccine contains antigen; body makes its own antibodies (active immunity)
Memory cells formed; second dose gives faster, stronger secondary response

stem: How does the human body respond when a vaccine is introduced into it? "Vaccination is a must for a healthy society." Justify.

model_answer:
*How much to write: 4–5 lines · 3 minutes*

A vaccine contains <u>antigenic proteins</u> of a pathogen or the <u>inactivated/weakened pathogen</u>. The body makes <mark>antibodies</mark> against these antigens, and also forms <mark>memory B and T cells</mark>. On a real infection the memory cells recognise the pathogen quickly and produce a massive antibody response.

**Why a must:** vaccination prevents infectious diseases and their spread; it has <u>eradicated smallpox</u> and brought polio, diphtheria, pneumonia and tetanus largely under control.

label: PYQ (2024)
stem: (i) Describe the life cycle of *Plasmodium* from the time it enters the human body until a female *Anopheles* mosquito bites the infected person. (ii) Mention two events of the life cycle that take place inside the female *Anopheles*.
hint: Sporozoites → liver → RBC → gametocytes.
model_answer:
*How much to write: 10 lines, as a numbered flow · 9 minutes*

**(i) In the human:**
1. *Plasmodium* enters as <mark>sporozoites</mark> (the infective form) with the saliva of an infected female *Anopheles*.
2. The sporozoites reach the <u>liver</u> and multiply asexually in liver cells.
3. They then attack the <u>red blood cells</u>, multiply asexually and <u>rupture</u> them.
4. Rupture releases the toxic <mark>haemozoin</mark>, which causes chill and high fever every three to four days.
5. Released parasites infect fresh RBCs; some develop into <u>gametocytes</u> (sexual stages) in the RBCs.
6. When a female *Anopheles* bites this person, she takes up the gametocytes with the blood meal.

**(ii) In the mosquito:**
- <mark>Fertilisation</mark> and development take place in the mosquito's gut (intestine).
- <u>Sporozoites</u> mature and move to the <u>salivary glands</u>, ready for the next bite.

:::tip Your answer must contain
- sporozoites → liver → RBC
- haemozoin and the fever cycle
- gametocytes taken up
- fertilisation in gut; sporozoites in salivary glands
:::

**Marks are lost for:** calling the mosquito the secondary host (it is where sexual reproduction occurs); leaving out the liver stage.

scheme.step: Sporozoites enter with the bite; multiply in liver cells
Attack and rupture RBCs; haemozoin causes chill and fever
Gametocytes develop in RBCs; taken up by female Anopheles
Fertilisation and development in mosquito gut

stem:
A graph shows the antibody concentration in a child's blood: a small rise after a vaccine is given, and a much higher, faster rise after infection by the same pathogen about four months later. (i) Why does the vaccine raise the antibody concentration? (ii) Why does it rise very fast after the later infection? (iii) Complete the table by identifying P, Q, R, S and T:
1. Natural active: antibodies made – yes; memory cells – **P**; attained by – **Q**.
2. Natural passive: antibodies made – no; memory cells – **R**; attained across the placenta or by breast-feeding.
3. Acquired (artificial) active: antibodies made – **S**; memory cells – yes; attained by vaccination.
4. Acquired (artificial) passive: antibodies made – **T**; memory cells – no; attained by an injection of antibodies.
hint: Primary vs secondary response; active = the body makes its own antibodies.
model_answer:
*How much to write: 3 lines each for (i) and (ii), five short entries for (iii) · 9 minutes*

**(i)** The vaccine carries the pathogen's <u>antigens</u> (or the weakened pathogen). B-lymphocytes respond by making antibodies: a <mark>primary response</mark>, slow and of low intensity.

**(ii)** The first exposure also left <mark>memory B and T cells</mark>. On meeting the same pathogen again they recognise it at once and produce a rapid, massive <u>secondary (anamnestic) response</u>.

**(iii)** P: <u>yes</u>. Q: <u>natural infection</u> (exposure to the pathogen). R: <u>no</u>. S: <u>yes</u>. T: <u>no</u>.

:::tip Your answer must contain
- primary response to antigen
- <mark>memory cells</mark> → secondary response
- P yes, Q infection, R no, S yes, T no
:::

**Marks are lost for:** saying passive immunity leaves memory cells.

scheme.step: Vaccine antigens cause a primary antibody response
Memory cells give a fast, strong secondary response
P, Q, R, S, T (½ each)

source_note: CBSE Class 12 Biology board paper 2023 (one set), reworded in our own words with our own answers. Official paper: cbse.gov.in → Question papers. The board question was based on a figure; it is described in words here.

label: PYQ (2023)
stem: (i) What is the chemical name of 'smack'? Why is taking it called abuse? (ii) Name the source plant and one effect on the human body of: marijuana, cocaine, morphine.
hint: Poppy, hemp, coca.
model_answer:
*How much to write: 8 lines or a 3-row table · 8 minutes*

**(i)** Smack is <mark>heroin, chemically diacetylmorphine</mark> (made by acetylation of morphine). It is a <u>depressant</u> that slows body functions. Taking it for a purpose other than medicinal use, in amounts or frequency that impair physical, physiological or psychological functions, is <u>drug abuse</u>; it is highly addictive.

**(ii)**

| Drug | Source plant | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| Marijuana | <u>*Cannabis sativa*</u> | affects the cardiovascular system |
| Cocaine | <u>*Erythroxylum coca*</u> | stimulates the CNS: euphoria, more energy; hallucinations in excess |
| Morphine | <u>*Papaver somniferum*</u> (poppy latex) | sedative and painkiller |

:::tip Your answer must contain
- <mark>diacetylmorphine</mark>; depressant; non-medical use
- three source plants
- one effect each
:::

**Marks are lost for:** mixing up the three plants; calling cocaine a depressant.

scheme.step: Why abuse: non-medical use impairing functions; depressant, addictive
